standards.description: Help students create and interpret bar charts, pie charts, and two-way frequency tables, including marginal and conditional distributions.
standards.ccssText: Construct and interpret bar charts, pie charts, and two-way frequency tables; compute and interpret joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies; identify association patterns in categorical data.

standards.description: Guide students to create and interpret dotplots, stemplots, histograms, and boxplots, describing shape, center, spread, and outliers.
standards.ccssText: Create and interpret dotplots, stemplots, histograms, and boxplots for quantitative data; describe distributions in terms of shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), center, spread, and outliers.

standards.description: Help students calculate and compare mean and median, understanding which measure is more resistant to outliers and skewness.
standards.ccssText: Calculate and compare the mean and median as measures of center; explain why the mean is sensitive to outliers and skewness while the median is resistant; choose the appropriate measure for a given context.

standards.description: Teach students to calculate range, IQR, variance, and standard deviation, and apply the 1.5xIQR rule to identify outliers.
standards.ccssText: Calculate range, interquartile range (IQR), variance, and standard deviation; apply the 1.5×IQR rule to identify outliers; compare distributions using measures of spread.

standards.description: Guide students to compare two or more distributions by discussing shape, center, spread, and unusual features in context.
standards.ccssText: Compare two or more distributions of quantitative data using graphical displays (back-to-back stemplots, parallel boxplots) and summary statistics; always comment on shape, center, spread, and outliers in context.

standards.description: Teach students to construct scatterplots, describe direction, form, and strength, and calculate and interpret the correlation coefficient r.
standards.ccssText: Construct and interpret scatterplots for bivariate data; describe direction, form, and strength of association; calculate the correlation coefficient r and interpret its value, noting that correlation does not imply causation.

standards.description: Guide students to find and interpret the equation of the least-squares regression line, including slope and y-intercept in context.
standards.ccssText: Determine the equation of the least-squares regression line; interpret the slope as the predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable; interpret the y-intercept; use the line for prediction.

standards.description: Help students calculate residuals and use residual plots to assess whether a linear model is appropriate for the data.
standards.ccssText: Calculate and interpret residuals as observed minus predicted; construct and analyze residual plots to assess the appropriateness of a linear model; identify patterns suggesting a non-linear model.

standards.description: Teach students to apply logarithmic and power transformations to linearize curved data and interpret results in the original units.
standards.ccssText: Apply logarithmic and power transformations to linearize curved data; interpret the LSRL of the transformed data in the context of the original variables; use the model to make predictions on the original scale.

standards.description: Help students distinguish between population and sample and compare simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling designs while identifying sources of bias.
standards.ccssText: Distinguish between population and sample; describe and compare simple random, stratified, cluster, and systematic sampling methods; identify sources of bias including voluntary response, undercoverage, and nonresponse.

standards.description: Guide students to distinguish between observational studies and experiments, explaining why only experiments can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
standards.ccssText: Distinguish between observational studies and controlled experiments; explain why experiments can establish causation while observational studies can only show association; identify confounding variables.

standards.description: Teach students the principles of good experimental design: randomization, replication, control, and blinding, including completely randomized and block designs.
standards.ccssText: Identify and apply the principles of experimental design: randomization, replication, control, and blinding; distinguish between completely randomized designs and randomized block designs; explain the role of a placebo and double-blinding.

standards.description: Help students interpret probability as long-run relative frequency and apply the complement, addition, and multiplication rules for independent events.
standards.ccssText: Interpret probability as long-run relative frequency; apply the complement rule P(A^c) = 1 - P(A), the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and the multiplication rule for independent events P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B).

standards.description: Teach students to calculate and interpret conditional probabilities and apply the general multiplication rule using two-way tables and tree diagrams.
standards.ccssText: Calculate and interpret conditional probability P(B|A); apply the general multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); use two-way tables and tree diagrams to find probabilities; distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events.

standards.description: Guide students to define discrete and continuous random variables and calculate and interpret the mean and standard deviation of a discrete random variable.
standards.ccssText: Define discrete and continuous random variables; construct probability distributions for discrete random variables; calculate and interpret the mean (expected value) and standard deviation; apply rules for means and variances of linear combinations.

standards.description: Help students identify binomial settings, calculate probabilities using the binomial formula, and find the mean and standard deviation of a binomial random variable.
standards.ccssText: Identify binomial settings (fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independence); calculate binomial probabilities using P(X = k) = C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and technology; find mean mu = np and standard deviation sigma = sqrt(np(1-p)).

standards.description: Describe properties of normal distributions, apply the 68-95-99.7 rule, and calculate probabilities and find values using z-scores and technology.
standards.ccssText: Describe properties of the normal distribution (symmetric, bell-shaped, defined by mean and standard deviation); apply the 68-95-99.7 empirical rule; standardize values using z = (x - mu)/sigma; use standard normal tables or technology to find probabilities and percentiles.

standards.description: Help students interpret confidence levels and intervals for a population parameter and understand how sample size and confidence level affect margin of error.
standards.ccssText: Interpret a confidence interval as a range of plausible values for a population parameter; interpret the confidence level as the long-run capture rate; describe the effect of changing confidence level and sample size on the margin of error.

standards.description: Teach students to construct and interpret a confidence interval for a population proportion, verifying the required conditions first.
standards.ccssText: Construct a one-sample z interval for a population proportion p; check conditions (random, n is large enough: np-hat >= 10 and n(1-p-hat) >= 10, independence); interpret the interval in context.

standards.description: Guide students to construct and interpret a confidence interval for a population mean using the t-distribution when sigma is unknown.
standards.ccssText: Construct a one-sample t interval for a population mean mu when sigma is unknown; check conditions (random, normal/large sample, independence); use t* critical values with n-1 degrees of freedom; interpret the interval in context.

standards.description: Help students construct and interpret confidence intervals for the difference of two proportions or two means from independent samples.
standards.ccssText: Construct and interpret confidence intervals for the difference of two population proportions (p1 - p2) and the difference of two population means (mu1 - mu2) from independent samples; check conditions for each procedure.

standards.description: Teach students to state hypotheses, interpret p-values, make decisions, and understand the meaning and consequences of Type I and Type II errors.
standards.ccssText: State null and alternative hypotheses in words and symbols; interpret the p-value as the probability of observing data at least as extreme as those obtained, assuming H0 is true; make reject/fail-to-reject decisions; define and interpret Type I and Type II errors and power.

standards.description: Guide students to conduct one-sample z-tests for proportions and t-tests for means, checking conditions and interpreting results in context.
standards.ccssText: Conduct a one-sample z-test for a population proportion and a one-sample t-test for a population mean; check required conditions; calculate the test statistic and p-value; state conclusions in context.

standards.description: Teach students to conduct two-sample tests for the difference of proportions and the difference of means, interpreting results in context.
standards.ccssText: Conduct two-sample z-tests for difference of proportions and two-sample t-tests for difference of means from independent samples; check conditions; compute test statistics and p-values; state conclusions in context.

standards.description: Guide students to conduct chi-square goodness-of-fit tests and tests for association in two-way tables, checking conditions and interpreting results.
standards.ccssText: Conduct chi-square goodness-of-fit tests to compare observed to expected counts; conduct chi-square tests for homogeneity and independence in two-way tables; check expected counts >= 5; interpret results in context.

standards.description: Help students conduct a t-test for the slope of a regression line and construct a confidence interval for the slope, interpreting both in context.
standards.ccssText: Conduct a t-test for the slope beta of a population regression line; check conditions (linear, independent, normal, equal variance, random); construct and interpret a confidence interval for the slope; interpret the standard error of the slope.
